content:
Tea for two became a habit before either of us admitted it was a ritual.

Every evening after closing, Iroh poured one cup for me and one for himself. Some nights I sat in silence. Some nights I played pai sho. Once, I spent an entire hour arguing about whether a particular pastry was improved or ruined by sesame seeds.

“It is improved,” Iroh said.

“It is overwhelmed.”

“The sesame is subtle.”

“The sesame is shouting.”

“You have not met enough sesame.”

He had begun saving the corner table for me. I teased him about it. He denied it while moving the sign that said RESERVED whenever I arrived.

The routine gave the days a gentle shape. Work. Tea. Conversation. Sleep above the shop while Iroh's footsteps moved below.

I had stopped feeling like a guest.

Then a woman from the market began visiting every afternoon.

She was a merchant with bright scarves and a laugh that filled the shop. She knew Iroh from years before, when he had traveled through the city. She called him “General” in a teasing tone and touched his arm when she spoke.

The first time, I thought nothing of it.

The third time, I broke a cup.

The sound silenced the room.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

Iroh looked toward me. The merchant looked too.

“No harm done,” Iroh said. “The cup had a dramatic life.”

I cleaned the pieces. My fingers shook.

The merchant watched me. “You are new.”

“Not very.”

“I have not seen you before.”

“You were not looking.”

Iroh's eyebrows rose.

The merchant laughed. “I like this one.”

“I am not a tea blend,” I said.

“Everything is a blend.”

She looked at Iroh. “You have become selective.”

“I have become tired,” he replied.

The merchant ordered a pot to take home and left. The door closed behind her.

I carried the broken cup to the kitchen.

Iroh followed.

“Are you angry?” he asked.

“No.”

“You are washing a cup that no longer exists.”

I looked down. Water ran over my hands.

“I’m embarrassed.”

“Why?”

“Because I was jealous.”

Iroh turned off the water. “Jealousy is not a crime.”

“It felt ugly.”

“Fear often does.”

“You know her.”

“I do.”

“She knows the version of you from before the tea shop.”

“She knows a version.”

“She called you General.”

“Many people have.”

“She touched you.”

Iroh's expression remained calm, but his eyes became very gentle. “Would you like to touch me?”

The question made me look at him.

“That is not fair.”

“It is not a trick.”

“You cannot solve jealousy by offering me your arm.”

“No. But I can remind you that her familiarity does not create a claim on me.”

I folded the wet cloth. “Do you want her?”

“No.”

The answer was immediate.

“Did you ever?”

“Once. A very long time ago.”

“And now?”

“Now I look forward to one person's footsteps.”

My throat tightened.

“You are going to say it is me.”

“It is you.”

“You could be more subtle.”

“I have been subtle. You broke a cup.”

I looked away. “I don’t want you to stop seeing her because of me.”

“I will not.”

The directness steadied me.

“But I want to know where I stand,” I said.

“You stand beside me.”

“That’s a nice phrase.”

“It is also a location.”

“You’re impossible.”

“So I have been told.”

Iroh took my hands and dried them with a clean towel. His fingers moved slowly over my knuckles.

“I am not asking you to be without fear,” he said. “I am asking you to bring it to me before it becomes a story you believe without evidence.”

“What evidence do I have?”

“You have my time. My attention. My honesty. You have the room above my shop and a key to the back door.”

I looked at him. “You gave me a key?”

“You have been using it for two weeks.”

“I thought it was the kitchen key.”

“It opens the back door as well.”

“You could have told me.”

“I enjoy watching you discover things.”

“That is a terrible habit.”

“I am old. I have earned a few.”

I laughed despite myself.

He lifted my hand and kissed it. “You are not a replacement for anyone.”

“I know.”

“You are not competing with my past.”

“I know.”

“You are the person I am choosing now.”

The words made my eyes sting.

“Can I kiss you?” he asked.

I stepped closer. “You can.”

The kiss began in the kitchen, between shelves of tea and a bucket of broken pottery. Iroh's hand settled at my waist. I held the front of his vest, feeling the warmth beneath it.

He kissed me with patience, but not distance. His mouth moved over mine until the embarrassment softened into desire. When he pressed me gently against the counter, he paused.

“Still comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Do you wish to stop?”

“No.”

“Then we may continue.”

The tea shop was dark beyond the kitchen. The kettle had cooled. The city moved outside without knowing that my world had become a pair of hands, a careful question, and an answer I was allowed to change.

When Iroh finally drew back, his forehead rested against mine.

“The cup can be replaced,” he said.

“I know.”

“The important things are not so easily broken.”

“You are talking about us.”

“I am talking about trust.”

“That is less romantic.”

“It is more durable.”

I kissed him again.

The next morning, a new cup sat at my place at the corner table. It was painted with a green dragon and a small white lotus.

On the bottom, Iroh had written: FOR TEA, NOT FOR THROWING.

I kept it.

The cup became part of the shop's daily rhythm. Iroh placed it at my table before I arrived. I threatened to use it as evidence in every future argument. He claimed the painting made it impossible to throw.

“You could have made it ugly,” I said.

“I considered painting a kettle on it.”

“That would have been more accurate.”

“The dragon was more dignified.”

“You are the dragon.”

“I am a man who owns a tea shop.”

“You can be both.”

He studied me over the rim of his cup. “You have been listening.”

“Occasionally.”

“It is a good habit.”

The merchant with the bright scarves did not return for several days. When she did, she brought Iroh a bundle of dried flowers.

“For the shop,” she said.

“Thank you,” he replied.

She looked at me. “You are still here.”

“I am.”

“Good.”

I waited until she left before speaking.

“Good?”

Iroh arranged the flowers in a jar. “She was pleased.”

“That sounded like approval.”

“It was.”

“Does everyone in your life have opinions about us?”

“Everyone has opinions about everything.”

“That is not comforting.”

“It is freeing. Their opinions are abundant, but they are not commands.”

I looked at the cup with my name. “You are good at saying things I need to hear.”

“I try to say what is true.”

“How do I know?”

Iroh stepped closer. “You do not have to know all at once. Watch what I do when the truth is inconvenient.”

The answer was not a demand for trust. It was permission to let trust grow slowly.

I touched his sleeve. “I can do that.”

He turned his hand and caught my fingers.

“And I can watch what you do,” he said.

“What do I do?”

“You return. Even when you are embarrassed. Even when you are angry. Even when you believe you have made a mistake.”

“I return because you have good tea.”

“Of course.”

“And pastries.”

“Naturally.”

His smile was warm. The teasing was becoming a language of its own.

That evening, I washed the new cup by hand. Iroh stood beside me, drying it with a soft cloth.

“You do not have to keep it at the shop,” he said.

“I want to.”

“Why?”

I looked at the dragon and lotus painted around the rim. “Because it reminds me that I can be wanted without being swallowed.”

Iroh's expression changed. He set down the cloth.

“Come here,” he said.

“That sounded like an order.”

“Then consider it an invitation.”

I stepped into his arms.

The kiss was gentle. It lasted long enough for the kettle to cool and the last lantern outside to dim.

When I parted, Iroh rested his forehead against mine.

“You are not a cup,” he said.

“I am aware.”

“You are not something I can place safely on a shelf.”

“That would be uncomfortable.”

“You are a person who can leave.”

“I know.”

“And return.”

I smiled. “I know that too.”

He kissed me once more before the shop's bell announced a late customer.

I both stepped apart, laughing softly, and returned to work.

The new cup waited between us.

Its painted dragon faced the door. Its lotus faced meroh. I decided that was a good arrangement.

Iroh agreed.

The cup stayed safe.

So did the trust between us.
